Q: Overhead/Performance of C# IEnumerables implemented with yield return A:

In principle an iterator block generates a state machine similar to your example, but the details will be somewhat different. If you want to know the exact difference, compare the generated IL and or asm-code.

Code like this can be quite sensitive to things like compiler optimizations. Newer versions of .Net support things like tiered compilation and devirtualization that might affect performance.

You also need to be careful when making measurement. Just using a stopwatch and a loop may include jitting-times, so you need to do an initial warmup call to ensure everything is jitted when doing your measurements. Ofc, this is even more difficult to do correctly once tiered compilation is introduced, so the recommendation is to use Benchmark.Net if you want accurate numbers.

In an ideal world the compiler would produce optimal code regardless of how the source was written. But writing compilers is difficult, so there is usually a trade of between abstraction and performance. I.e. iterator blocks are very useful and convenient, but if you want the best performance it is usually better to stick to simple for/while loops.

Q: What is considered a cross-origin request A:

The request is cross-origin

The relevant information to determine if a request is cross-origin comes from the URL of the API, and from its origin (webapp origin is where the web application is loaded from).
In the question these URLs are:

  • (I suppose that) the URL of the POST request is http://example.com:3000
  • the URL of the origin of the webapp is http://example.com

The request is cross-origin because the origin of the webapp doesn't contain the port, so the value of the port in the origin is equal to 80, while the port in the POST request is 3000.
So while schema (http) and host (example.com) are the same, ports are different and this causes that the request is cross-origin.

Note about the error message

The message:

No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.  
Origin 'http://example.com' is therefore not allowed access.

means that:

  • the POST request contains the header: Origin: http://example.com
  • the response of the server doesn't send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header equal to * or which contains http://example.com.

Q: Extracting Data from Excel Database A:

Bare bones approach - could be optimized for better performance, but it will do the job.

Sub SplitToSheets()

Dim c As Range, ws As Worksheet, rngNames

    With ThisWorkbook.Sheets("EmployeeData")
        Set rngNames = .Range(.Range("A1"), .Cells(Rows.Count, 1).End(xlUp))
    End With

    For Each c In rngNames.Cells
        Set ws = GetSheet(ThisWorkbook, c.Value)
        c.EntireRow.Copy ws.Cells(Rows.Count, 1).End(xlUp).Offset(1, 0)
    Next c

End Sub


Function GetSheet(wb As Workbook, wsName As String, _
         Optional CreateIfMissing As Boolean = True) As Worksheet

    Dim ws As Worksheet
    On Error Resume Next
    Set ws = wb.Sheets(wsName)
    On Error GoTo 0

    If ws Is Nothing And CreateIfMissing Then
        Set ws = wb.Sheets.Add(after:=wb.Sheets(wb.Sheets.Count))
        ws.Name = wsName
    End If

    Set GetSheet = ws
End Function

Q: Trying to read CSV file , says "Error in nchar(x, "width") : invalid multibyte string, element 1" , how do fix this? A:

R recently returned a very similar error message (*) to me for a weekly batch of *.html files that rvest::read_html(x) has previously read into R without any problem.

(*)          “Error in nchar(x) : invalid multibyte string, element 1”

This unexpected error occurred directly after I upgraded to latest R-4.6.1 and ran Update Packages. The correct encoding name for these *.html files turned out to be: "UTF-16LE". Though confusing at first, the problem was quickly identified by using helper function rvest::guess_encoding(x) which returns a list of best guess encoding names in order of confidence level. In this case "UTF-16LE" came 3rd on the guess list, while all other listed encoding names completely failed to read the *.html files into R. See link for this excellent tidyverse helper function below:

https://rvest.tidyverse.org/reference/encoding.html

I’ve since successfully used rvest::guess_encoding(x) to help identify correct encoding names for reading into R *.html, *.htm, *.csv and *.txt files.
